source.title: SAFR: Neuron Redistribution for Interpretability
source.authors: Ruidi Chang; Chun-Yuan Deng; Hanjie Chen

record.tranche_reason: The study builds SAFR around the superposition and polysemanticity concepts to improve interpretability, but reports its own token-level allocation and deletion metrics rather than directly testing the claim about individual neurons.
record.gate_note: The reported capacity and SRS results concern token representations and token deletion, not whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. They are recorded as related findings, not as direct tests of a claim version.
record.test_reason: SAFR uses superposition/polysemanticity as a design concept. It reports only its own method's token-deletion SRS, accuracy and token-level capacity. Its 'polysemanticity' is a dot-product overlap between token hidden representations, not neurons responding to unrelated inputs. It does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons in any model, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude SAFR improves interpretability, as measured by SRS, without compromising prediction performance. They also say it offers a way to visualize neuron allocation. On IMDB, accuracy at the selected setting is slightly below baseline (78.45 vs 80.14).
record.recipe_differences: SAFR trains a text classifier with importance- and interaction-based loss regularizers; it does not reproduce the original neuron-level methods. It also inserts a VMASK layer and evaluates token-capacity deletion.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SRS and accuracy vary with the regularization coefficients λImp and λInter; the selected settings differ between SST-2 and IMDB.

fits_no_version.finding: In a single-layer transformer, SAFR regularization raised token-deletion SRS over the baseline at roughly comparable accuracy: SST-2 17.21 vs 4.00, IMDB 28.48 vs 3.54. VMASK-important tokens had higher token capacity than other tokens (0.5745 vs 0.1794 on SST-2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularizing token-representation overlap can raise a token-deletion interpretability score in small text classifiers without large accuracy loss.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The experiments use a single-layer transformer and two text-classification datasets. The authors note that more standardized evaluation metrics are needed and that SAFR does not fully explain causal mechanisms. No uncertainty estimates are reported; the SRS metric is a proxy based on token deletion rather than a direct neuron-level measure.
record.rows_left_out: The hyperparameter tables report additional settings and repeated values; these detailed ablation outcomes are not included because they remain token-level proxy results and do not directly measure any claim version.

untested.parts: No count or share of polysemantic MLP neurons, and no per-layer comparison of neuron polysemanticity.
No test of whether feature count exceeding neuron count causes polysemanticity.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization or training noise with enough capacity.
Loss regularization is varied, but the neuron polysemanticity share is not measured, and neither activation functions nor architectures are compared.
No reinterpretation of specific polysemantic neurons.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The study redefines polysemanticity and capacity over token hidden representations, extending Scherlis et al., rather than over individual neurons. Its results therefore cannot bear on the neuron-level claim. Accuracy on SST-2 is low (about 70%) for a single-layer model with random embeddings. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or individual vision neuron is studied.
The study uses a single-layer transformer for text classification, but does not measure polysemanticity of MLP neurons across tokens or contexts in language models.
No test of whether feature count exceeds neuron capacity or whether capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is sufficient capacity.
Regularization is varied, but the study does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons or compare activation functions or architectures.
No investigation of whether apparently mixed individual neurons share a feature or job.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons as polysemantic.
